title: Reductivity is inherited by smooth connected quotient groups over a field
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field] [def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $H,J$ be smooth connected affine $k$-group schemes of finite type [def-sc-group-scheme] [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] [def-weil-connected-scheme] [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. A group here is reductive if it has no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent closed subgroup; unipotent means admitting a faithful matrix representation by unipotent matrices. If $q:H\to J$ is a faithfully flat homomorphism and $H$ is reductive, then $J$ is reductive. No condition of centrality, connectedness or smoothness is imposed on the scheme-theoretic kernel.

source.place: Section 1.1, discussion of unipotent radicals and surjections adjacent to Definition 1.1.11, printed pp.10--11: images of reductive groups are reductive, including surjections with nonsmooth kernels. WANTED locally as literature/conrad-reductive-group-schemes.pdf.

proof.text: Let $U\subseteq J$ be any smooth connected normal unipotent closed subgroup. Form $P=H\times_JU$ with projections $p:P\to H$ and $r:P\to U$ by [def-pc-fibre-product]. The map $p$ is a closed immersion by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-base-change]; thus $P$ is affine of finite type, since its coordinate ring is a quotient of $k[H]$ by [def-weil-closed-immersion]. On every $k$-algebra $A$, $P(A)$ identifies with $\{h\in H(A):q(h)\in U(A)\}$, a normal subgroup of $H(A)$ because $U(A)$ is normal in $J(A)$ [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. This also constructs its group structure and both projection homomorphisms. Since $J$ is smooth and $q$ is faithfully flat, [lem-sfb-affine-group-homomorphism-image] makes $H(k)\to J(k)$ surjective. For each $u\in U(k)$ choose $h$ with $q(h)=u$; the pair $(h,u)$ gives an element of $P(k)$ mapping to $u$. Hence $r:P(k)\to U(k)$ is surjective, even if $P$ or $\ker q$ is nonreduced.

source.place: Proposition 5.47, p.110, rational-point surjectivity; inverse-image subgroup construction. Agent assembly, using Stacks Tag 01QR (morphisms-lemma-base-change-closed-immersion).

proof.text: Put $C=P^0$ and $M=C_{\mathrm{red}}$. By [lem-sfb-locally-algebraic-group-identity-component], $C$ is open and closed in $P$, and $M$ is a smooth connected integral group scheme of finite type with $|M|=|C|$. Both are closed in $P$, so $M$ is a closed subgroup of $H$ and is affine: on affine coordinates the successive inclusions are quotient maps, whose composite is again a quotient [def-weil-closed-immersion]. For $h\in H(k)$, normality of $P$ makes conjugation by $h$ an automorphism of $P$ fixing its identity. Such an automorphism preserves its identity component and its open-subscheme structure, and preserves the nilradical on every affine chart. It therefore preserves $M$ as a closed subgroup scheme. Since $H$ is smooth and $k$ is algebraically closed, [lem-sfb-smooth-ambient-normality-geometric] implies that $M$ is normal in $H$ as a subgroup scheme, on all test algebras. No smoothness of $P$ was used.

source.place: Proposition 1.34, pp.16--17; reduced identity subgroup as in Stacks Tags 0B7R, 047R and 047P/047N; preservation by conjugation is the agent argument written here.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-connected-normal-subgroup-reductive], $M$ is reductive: it is a smooth connected closed normal subgroup of the reductive group $H$. Restrict $r$ to $f:M\to U$. The unipotence assumed for $U$ gives, by [lem-sfb-geometric-unipotence-unitriangular-embedding], a closed embedding of $U$ into an upper unitriangular group. Let $T$ be any maximal $k$-torus of $M$. Since $k$ is algebraically closed, $T\simeq\mathbf G_m^d=D_k(\mathbf Z^d)$; the last identification sends the group-algebra basis monomials to Laurent monomials. Apply [lem-sfb-diagonalizable-to-unipotent-trivial] to $f|_T$ and that embedding of $U$. It gives $f|_T=1$ as a homomorphism of group schemes, not just on rational points.

source.place: Corollary 21.53, p.441, normal-subgroup reductivity; Corollary 14.12 and Theorem 14.5, pp.281--283, unitriangular form; Corollary 14.18(b), p.284, vanishing of multiplicative-to-unipotent homomorphisms.

proof.text: Let $K=\ker(f)\subseteq M$, a closed subgroup with $K(A)=\ker(f(A))$ by [lem-sc-kernel-subgroup]. Step 3 says every maximal torus $T$ of $M$ is contained in $K$. By [lem-sfb-reductive-torus-self-centralizer], $C_M(T)=T$ scheme-theoretically for every such $T$. The algebraically closed field $k$ is infinite: if it were finite, $1+\prod_{a\in k}(X-a)$ would be a nonconstant polynomial without a root. All hypotheses of [lem-sfb-cartan-subgroups-generate] hold for the smooth connected affine finite-type group $M$ over $k$; geometric connectedness is connectedness here because $k$ is algebraically closed. Every Cartan subgroup $C_M(T)$ is contained in $K$, so that node gives $K=M$. Thus $f=1$ on every test algebra. This includes $M=1$ and the rank-zero case.

source.place: Proposition 17.61(a), p.372, self-centralizer; Theorem 17.91, p.381, generation by Cartan subgroups. Agent application to the closed kernel, with no reductivity-of-quotients input.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-group-neutral-component-translates] to $P$. There are finitely many components, each a translate $g_iC$ for a point $g_i\in P(k)$. Every $k$-point of $C$ factors through its reduction $M$: its map from an affine coordinate ring to the field $k$ kills all nilpotents. Conversely every $M(k)$-point is a $C(k)$-point, so $C(k)=M(k)$. On $P(k)$ the homomorphism $r$ is therefore constant on each component: if $x=g_im$ with $m\in M(k)$, then $r(x)=r(g_i)f(m)=r(g_i)$ by step 4. Thus $r(P(k))$ is finite. Step 1 gives $r(P(k))=U(k)$, so $U(k)$ is finite. This passage uses the components of the possibly nonreduced inverse image $P$, not a smoothness assumption on its kernel.

source.place: Proposition 1.34 and Corollary 1.35, pp.16--18, finitely many translates of the identity component; elementary reduction and rational-point calculation.

proof.text: Write $A=k[U]$. Smoothness implies reducedness by [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced] and [def-pc-reduced-scheme]. Since $U$ is connected, $U^0=U$; [lem-sfb-locally-algebraic-group-identity-component] therefore identifies $U=(U^0)_{\mathrm{red}}$ as integral. Thus $A$ is a domain. The finite set $S=U(k)$ is nonempty because it contains the identity. For any $a\in A$, form $b=\prod_{s\in S}(a-a(s))\in A$, with $a(s)\in k$ viewed as scalars. The function $b$ vanishes at every $k$-point, so $b=0$ by [lem-wf-affine-nullstellensatz-vanishing], which applies to the finitely generated reduced $k$-algebra $A$. A product in a domain is zero only if one factor is zero; hence $a=a(s)$ for some $s$. Every element of $A$ is therefore scalar. The identity point splits $k\to A$, so $A=k$ and $U=\operatorname{Spec}k$ is the trivial subgroup. Every smooth connected normal unipotent closed subgroup of $J$ is trivial; together with the stated smoothness, connectedness, affineness and finite type, this is exactly reductivity of $J$.

source.place: Propositions 1.10--1.12, pp.8--9, density/vanishing of functions at rational points; smooth connected reduction as in Stacks 0B7R, 047R and 047P/047N; smooth reducedness Tag 056T. Agent finite-point argument.
